title: Car Pooling
summary: A car drives east with capacity seats. Each trip [passengers, from, to] picks people up at km from and drops them at km to. Return whether every trip fits.
statement:
A car has `capacity` empty seats and only drives east. Each `trips[i] = [passengers, from, to]` picks up `passengers` people at kilometre `from` and drops them off at kilometre `to`.

Return `true` if the car can complete every trip without ever carrying more than `capacity` passengers. People dropped off at a point free their seats for people picked up at the same point.
constraints: Each trip is [passengers, from, to] with 1 ≤ passengers ≤ 100 and 0 ≤ from < to ≤ 1000
hints: Only the points where people get on or off matter.
Use a difference array over kilometres 0 … 1000: add passengers at from and subtract them at to.
Take a running sum along the road; if it ever exceeds capacity, return false. Sorting the pickup and drop-off events works when the road is long.
explain: Between locations 3 and 5 both trips are in the car: 2 + 3 = 5 passengers, more than the capacity of 4. So the answer is `false`.

title: Range Sum Query - Mutable
summary: NumArray(nums) supports update(index, val) and sumRange(left, right) (inclusive), both in O(log n).

perf.label: n = 100,000 with 100,000 operations
perf.call: NumArray na = new NumArray(BCB.ints(100000, -100, 100)); long sum = 0; for (int q = 0; q < 100000; q++) { if (BCB.R.nextBoolean()) na.update(BCB.rnd(0, 99999), BCB.rnd(-100, 100)); else { int l = BCB.rnd(0, 99999); sum += na.sumRange(l, BCB.rnd(l, 99999)); } } Object r = sum;

statement:
Implement `NumArray`:

- `NumArray(int[] nums)` stores the array,
- `void update(int index, int val)` sets `nums[index]` to `val`,
- `int sumRange(int left, int right)` returns the sum of `nums[left..right]`, both ends inclusive.

Both `update` and `sumRange` must run in O(log n). The tests call the class with a list of operations and their arguments.
constraints: 0 ≤ index < nums.length and 0 ≤ left ≤ right < nums.length
At most 10^5 calls to update and sumRange
hints: A prefix-sum array answers queries in O(1) but an update can change O(n) prefix sums.
A Fenwick tree (binary indexed tree) supports "add delta at i" and "sum of the first i" in O(log n).
update(index, val) adds val − nums[index]; sumRange(l, r) = prefix(r + 1) − prefix(l). A segment tree also works.
explain: The sum of `[1,3,5]` is 9. After `update(1, 2)` the array is `[1,2,5]`, so the sum becomes 8. Output: `[null,9,null,8]`.

title: Count of Smaller Numbers After Self
summary: For each element, count how many elements to its right are strictly smaller.
statement:
For each element `nums[i]`, count how many elements to its right are strictly smaller than it. Return those counts as a list, in the original order.

Counting by brute force is O(n²). Merge sort, counting how many elements from the right half jump ahead of each left element, gives O(n log n); a Fenwick tree works too.
hints: Checking every pair is O(n²). Process the array from right to left, asking "how many values seen so far are smaller?"
With values in [−10⁴, 10⁴], shift them to [1, 20001] and use a Fenwick tree over values: query the count below nums[i], then add nums[i].
Merge sort on indices also works: while merging, count how many elements from the right half move before each left-half element.
explain: To the right of 5 are 2 and 1 (2 smaller), right of 2 is 1 (1), right of 6 is 1 (1), and nothing is right of 1 (0). The answer is `[2,1,1,0]`.

title: Reverse Pairs
summary: Count pairs i < j with nums[i] > 2 · nums[j]. Values span the full 32-bit range, so watch for overflow.

perf.label: n = 50,000 across the full int range
perf.gen: int[] a0 = new int[50000]; for (int i = 0; i < a0.length; i++) a0[i] = BCB.R.nextInt();

statement:
A reverse pair is a pair of indices `(i, j)` with `i < j` and `nums[i] > 2 × nums[j]`. Return the number of reverse pairs in `nums`.

Values span the full 32-bit range, so `2 × nums[j]` can overflow an `int`.
hints: Counting pairs where an earlier element beats a later one is the inversion-counting pattern, solved with merge sort.
During merge sort, before merging two sorted halves, count for each left element how many right elements satisfy left > 2 × right, using a pointer that only moves forward.
Do the multiplication in long. Then merge the halves as usual.
explain: A reverse pair needs `nums[i] > 2 × nums[j]` with `i < j`. Both 3s are greater than 2 × 1 for the 1 at the end, and no other pair qualifies, so the answer is 2.

title: Count of Range Sum
summary: Count the contiguous subarrays whose sum lies in [lower, upper] (inclusive). Sums can exceed 32 bits.
statement:
Count the contiguous subarrays of `nums` whose sum lies in the range `[lower, upper]`, inclusive.

Sums can exceed the 32-bit range, so use 64-bit arithmetic.

A subarray sum is the difference of two prefix sums. So count pairs of prefix sums whose difference lies in the range, using merge sort or an ordered structure.
hints: With prefix sums P, subarray (i, j] has sum P[j] − P[i]. You need, for each j, the number of earlier i with P[j] − upper ≤ P[i] ≤ P[j] − lower.
Merge sort on the prefix sums counts these pairs: for each element of the right half, two pointers find the matching range in the sorted left half.
Use long for the prefix sums. A Fenwick tree over compressed prefix values works too.
explain: The subarrays `[-2]` (sum -2), `[-1]` (sum -1) and `[-2,5,-1]` (sum 2) fall inside [-2, 2]. Every other subarray contains the 5 and sums higher, so the answer is 3.

title: Create Sorted Array through Instructions
summary: Insert values one by one into a sorted container. Each insert costs min(#existing values smaller, #existing values larger). Return the total cost modulo 10^9 + 7.
statement:
Start with an empty container and insert the values of `instructions` one by one, keeping the container sorted. Inserting a value costs the minimum of:

- the number of values already in the container that are strictly less than it, and
- the number already in the container that are strictly greater than it.

Return the total cost of all insertions, modulo `10^9 + 7`.
hints: For each insertion you need two counts over the values inserted so far: how many are smaller and how many are larger.
Keep a Fenwick tree indexed by value (values go up to 10⁵). smaller = prefix(v − 1); larger = inserted so far − prefix(v).
Add min(smaller, larger) to the answer modulo 10⁹ + 7, then add v to the tree.
explain: Inserting 1, 5 and 6 costs 0 each: nothing already present is both smaller and larger. Inserting 2 finds one smaller value (1) and two larger (5, 6), costing min(1, 2) = 1. The total is 1.

title: Falling Squares
summary: Squares [left, side] drop one at a time onto the x-axis and stick where they land (touching edges don't support). After each drop, return the height of the tallest stack so far.
statement:
Squares are dropped one at a time onto the x-axis. Each `positions[i] = [left, side]` is a square with side length `side` whose left edge is at `left`. It falls straight down until it lands on the x-axis or on top of an earlier square, and then stays there. Squares that only touch at an edge do not support each other.

After each square lands, record the height of the tallest stack so far. Return those heights.
constraints: Each square is [left, side] with 1 ≤ left ≤ 10⁸ and 1 ≤ side ≤ 10⁶
hints: A square covers the half-open interval [left, left + side). It lands on the highest existing square that overlaps that interval.
With at most 1000 squares, an O(n²) solution is fine: for each new square, check every earlier square for overlap and take the maximum height.
Its new height is that maximum + side. Keep a running maximum for the answer. A segment tree with coordinate compression is the scalable version.
explain: The first square lands at height 2. The second overlaps it and lands on top, reaching 2 + 3 = 5. The third falls on empty ground at height 1, so the tallest stack stays 5: `[2,5,5]`.
